item.title: Spotlighting Patience: A Core Superpower
item.description:
Parenting

Spotlighting Patience: A Core Superpower

Why true patience is an active and adaptive skill, not just restraint.

Posted July 31, 2026

Source: chalermphon_tiam/Shutterstock

I have spent a lot of time thinking about patience especially since I completed my days of hands-on mothering. When I look back on this time, I distinctly remember regular feelings of impatience. This was often connected with pressure to complete a task or trying to live up to some external expectation or obligation. It was often at a cost of being present and staying in the moment with my child. I now understand that impatience was one of my Achilles heels which likely explains why I am drawn to write about it. I grew up not really valuing or understanding the power of patience.

Now I understand patience as an active dynamic, an intentionality. It is the ability to remain grounded, to stay present, when our outer and inner world threaten to destabilize us. A knowledge that in time things will work out and will be ok—somehow. It encourages us to respond with calm and fortitude and to shape a space to wait, rather than defaulting to an unthinking reaction when confronting uncertainty. It requires us to be generous with ourselves and others and not to rush, to persevere and endure. Patience values mindfulness, deliberation and thoughtfulness, while rushing is questionable. It prizes respect and forgiveness, and maintains an elastic rather than rigid attitude toward time. It accepts that interruption and challenges are part of everyday life.

It favors flow rather than rigidity.

Hands-on moms and patience: A contradiction in terms?

I continue to be curious about how hands-on moms who may be managing sleepless nights, and/or the tantrums of toddlers, and/or the trials of a tween who is being bullied, and/or a teenager who stays out all night and doesn't inform you can possibly manage all this with patience and stay present? What are the barriers to patience? Patience forces us to face and negotiate uncertainty and to remain present when it may be easier to shut down. When our bodies rail against being patient. This can be scary and counterintuitive on so many levels.

No wonder patience is so sorely tested in hands-on mothering. The lived maternal experience stands out as a robust gauge of patience. The social expectations placed on mothers and how they collude with these ideals are core to mothering and grounded in the unique and impossible fantasies attached to mothering, such as unlimited patience. This is maintained by society, including the mothers themselves, and buoyed by the current cultural subscription to instant gratification.

In line with my work on maternal ambivalence. Moms are both patient and impatient, calm and harassed, composed and erratic. I marvel at the patience shown by hands-on mums, and I identify with and understand the lack of patience they show. Patience levels shift on a continuum which relies on time and variables linked to external and internal dynamics. Outer variables include how much support the mother receives from her partner, her family or other help, how sleep deprived she may be, her current economic and social situation. Her particular emotional experience includes her own historical experience of patience, how it has been modeled to her and how natural it is for her.

So how do we integrate and practice patience, especially if it’s not part of our inborn temperament?

A few hints:

  1. Find a rhythm of patience by making a conscious decision to learn to be patient and present with ourselves.
  • Slow down and develop a bodily awareness of when we are rushing and feeling pressured and ask whether this is serving me well.
  • Find a way to slow down the world for a minute. Make a distinction between responding and reacting to demands, both internal and external. Responding means choosing to wait and think, rather than immediately answering or acting. This involves unsubscribing to instant gratification.
  • Use the times when we lose our cool as a way to learn about ourselves, our bodily signals and triggers. Rather than reprimanding ourselves, be forgiving. We can arrive at patience, but it takes time, many missteps and backward movement along the way. When we “win,” let’s pat ourselves on the back.
  1. Make a concerted effort to understand our personal relationship with patience and time. How do we think about time? Or do we? Are we aware of how it commands our days? Does time dominate us or are we in sync with it? Do we put so many commitments into our day that our patience becomes sorely tested? Are we willing to confront and change these behaviors?
  2. Recognize that social media and its emphasis on instant gratification are tricky. They erode and improve our lives. Let’s continually monitor their worth and see how they pervade our internal and external world, dysregulate and distort us and are a barrier to patience.
  3. Let’s introduce some truthful sayings that are helpful with patience:
  • Life is messy and interrupted
  • We learn from our missteps
  • We make it up as we go along
  • We are all muddling through

Flow is fundamental to patience. Words and concepts such as leaning into our struggles and missteps, forgiveness, acceptance, slowing down and presence are intentional and fluid.

In my first book1 I wrote a section if only. In hindsight, I was talking about my previous lack of patience and how it affected my emotional presence in my hands-on mothering days. I was so overcome with doing that I often missed out on emotionally being in the space.

If only I had spent more time playing and laughing with my children, being less serious, enjoyed longer bubble bath times, being late to school more often, going to buy an ice cream instead of after-school activities.

It has taken me years to recognize the true meaning of patience and to hone this skill.

So far I’m working toward being proficient at it and I think I’m doing ok.

P.S. Let’s grant hands-on moms some grace and latitude.

It's impossible to hold it together all the time but a little patience goes a long way.

item.title: 5 Tough Lessons I’ve Learned From Mania
item.description:
Mania

5 Tough Lessons I’ve Learned From Mania

Personal Perspective: Knowledge gleaned from battling bipolar disorder.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • The extremes of mania are usually the source of its danger; more is not always better.
  • Following the rules and respecting authority is difficult but essential when you’re manic.
  • Hard as it is, exercising caution and moderation can save you from serious consequences.

I’ve lived with bipolar disorder all my life, so I feel I can speak with some authority on mania. Mania is a great teacher, because its lessons are often very dramatic. You’d think they’d therefore stick in your head, and never need repeating. Unfortunately, that’s rarely the case—when the next manic episode hits, you forget all the hard-won wisdom of the past because you’re so much smarter, more insightful, more incandescent now.

Here are five lessons I’ve learned the hard way from my journeys into and out of mania:

1. Sometimes it’s best just to go with the stupid flow

I'm all for thinking outside the box—and mental illness, especially mania, enables you to do that. When I’m manic, I can envision all sorts of amazing possibilities for the future, and see all sorts of flaws in the status quo; and I’m not the least bit shy about proposing big changes or just making them without asking first.

I remember when I was an entertainment attorney working on a major studio lawsuit, not getting near enough sleep to stay stable. I had a manic epiphany one night that the voluminous case files (we’re talking thousands of pages) should be rearranged according to date, not alphabetically. So I stayed up all night and proudly showed off my results to the Evil Partner I worked for the next morning. He had a conniption fit: “That’s a paralegal’s job, and don’t you dare think you can bill for it.”

Then he ordered me to put all the files back the way they’d been, only to make the paralegal rearrange them according to date before trial.

The thing is, most of us don't live on the Apple campus, where fantastic flights of innovation land you a bonus and a corner office. Alas, most of us live in the real world, which respects—and expects—conformity, or at the very least, respect for the hierarchy.

What I’ve learned: You should run your manic brilliance by someone you trust before acting on it.

2. Rules are not suggestions

“Prescription” is an interesting word. I looked it up—it means an edict, a law, an order. In other words, a rule. Nine times out of ten, the label on a prescribed psychiatric drug says, “Do not take with alcohol.” Ten times out of ten, I considered that merely a suggestion, and continued to drink while taking my meds.

Looking back, that was probably the stupidest thing I’ve ever done in my life. It not only got me in trouble with the law, but the alcohol messed up my brain chemistry and prevented my meds from working. It wasn’t until I got sober that I finally got sane.

Like clichés, rules often exist for a reason, and that reason is usually to keep you or someone else safe. You never see a big red road sign that says, "Please consider stopping here if you feel like it, okay?"

What I’ve learned: Breaking a rule may just leave you broken.

3. Binge-anything is bad

Binge-eating makes you sick. Binge-watching makes you stupid. There is such a thing as binge-happy, too. It’s that state where you’re too, too wonderful for words and the sky’s the limit for your magnificent mood. I know, I know—it feels amazing, and I hate to advise you to dull it down with lithium or one of the newer antipsychotic drugs. But it’s dangerous to fly too close to the sun; it will burn you up before you can reach it. That’s what your meds are for—to keep your feet on the ground.

Binge-everything comes naturally to those of us on the bipolar spectrum, and moderation may seem like an impossible goal. So don't shoot for perfect moderation. That's an oxymoron, and it’s sure to set you up for failure.

What I’ve learned: Try to moderate moderately.

4. Xanax has an evil twin

It's the Xanax you take after the Xanax you took begins to wear off. The second, or third, or fourth Xanax in a row. Just because the pills are a pretty pale blue doesn't make them innocent playthings. In fact, one of the most grueling things I’ve ever witnessed is someone struggling to recover from Xanax abuse. It’s called benzodiazepine detox for a reason. They're toxic.

This applies to all psychoactive drugs. When you’re manic, it always feels like more would be better. Isn’t it strange, though, that you’re the only one who seems to think that more is such a good idea? True, you’re the expert on your own body, but you’re not an expert on dosage or restraint.

What I’ve learned: Your doctor is your Jiminy Cricket. Listen to him—that’s why you’re paying him money.

5. There's no such thing as instant intimacy

For some inexplicable reason, mania can make you irresistible to others. (At first, that is, until it wears them out.) Sudden sexy is very seductive, and it’s hard not to want to exploit that chemistry for all it’s worth. But locking eyes too much, too hard, too often across a crowded room can give you a major headache later. Charisma always has consequences.

You may be charming when you’re manic, but your judgment about people and propriety is non-existent. Never trust it. Because no matter how warm and fuzzy you feel, bosses aren't magically your besties. Policemen aren't your pals.

What I’ve learned: Be wary about disclosing secrets to people you’ve just met. Strangers are strange for a reason—you don’t know them.

In sum, my overall manic lesson is really quite simple. Going to extremes is usually just that: too extreme. If you don’t believe me, ask Icarus.

item.title: What Aging Parents Want Their Adult Children to Understand
item.description:
Aging

What Aging Parents Want Their Adult Children to Understand

Patience, honest conversation, and respect can deepen family connection.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Aging parents want to be known for who they are now, not only who they once were.
  • Early talks about health, housing, and end-of-life wishes can prevent conflict later.
  • Hovering and unsolicited advice can feel controlling, even when motivated by love.
  • Open-ended questions and patient listening help aging parents feel safe enough to open up.

One of the most powerful experiences we can have as human beings is the feeling of being understood. There is nothing quite like looking into another person's eyes and seeing that they really get us. They listen to what we have to say and truly understand how we feel—no judgment, quick fixes, or unsolicited advice.

To feel seen, met, listened to, and understood is the basis for all loving relationships. And our ever-changing relationship with our aging parents is no exception.

Below are some of the most common things aging parents say they want and need, and a few helpful reminders:

1. Get to know me in this new season of my life

We are all older versions of who we were years ago in our families of origin. The father or mother who once lived in the family home has entered a new season of life as well that may now include sons- and daughters-in-law, grandchildren, and changes in how we look, feel, and live.

With these changes come unlimited opportunities to become better or lesser versions of ourselves. We may make the most of our family relationships or avoid taking the time and making the effort to honestly understand what is happening in one another's lives—and squander those opportunities.

Whether or not they admit it, most parents want to be loved, understood, and supported as they get older. Being able to enjoy good times together, support one another in tough times, and live in peace with their adult children are, they will tell you, "a blessing."

2. Please make time to talk openly with me about our lives

There are sensitive, "elephant in the room" matters involving everything from health and estate planning to living arrangements and how our parents want things to go as they get older and after they die.

Opening the lines of communication, getting these matters out on the table, discussing them, and reaching decisions whenever possible clears the air of tension and uncertainty — and allows us to enjoy our time together more fully. Discussing and handling most of the important matters can also prevent family members from finding themselves in complete chaos and confusion when a mother or father dies.

3. Yes, we have differences. Let's please work through them peacefully

We may be members of the same family, connected by genetics, history, values, and experience, but we are all different by our very nature.

When we treat one another with loving kindness, patience, and understanding, we create opportunities for closeness, fun, and good times spent sharing food, feelings, music, memories, and holidays. Turning the pages of life together, acknowledging our differences, remaining humble and forgiving one another's imperfections, we make it possible to disagree, get angry, apologize, heal our wounds, and feel grateful for the gifts and good times. Doing this also helps us make peace with the circle of life as we all move through time.

A few important reminders

No hovering
We have all heard about "helicopter parents." Aging parents do not like being hovered over by their adult children any more than adult children like being hovered over by their parents.

A 68-year-old client who began seeing me after the death of her husband recently told me, "It's been a year since my husband died, and if my son and daughter don't stop calling me 10 times a day to see if I'm OK, I'm going to kill them."

Another parent told me she felt "suffocated" by her adult son after being diagnosed with early-stage Alzheimer's.

"It was enough to find out that I had Alzheimer's," she said. "What my son is doing to make me feel better is making me feel worse. I'm not sure how to get him to back off and lighten up."
Love, support, and caregiving are wonderful. Don't overdo it.

Ask, don't assume
An honest conversation that begins with a few open-ended questions—and diligent listening—can provide adult children with the information they need to understand what their parent wants and does not want.

The questions must be honest inquiries, rather than the kind of fake questions that disguise criticism, judgment, and/or opinion. A parent who has not figured out what they want and need as they have gotten older may need your help patiently unearthing how they feel, what they want, and a few good options for their futures.

Asking rather than assuming and listening patiently demonstrates authentic curiosity, interest, respect, and a desire to understand. Saying and doing these things help parents feel loved and safe enough to open up.

Be patient and be with me
It is easy to become triggered by the emotional rawness that accompanies unwelcome losses, changes, and challenges within a family. But impatience, disinterest, and disrespect rarely end well or result in productive decision-making.

Your best approach when having difficult conversations with family members is to lead with patience, empathy, kindness, and understanding. Sometimes the most helpful thing we can do is to slow down and simply be with one another, without rushing to fix or resolve everything.

Start with the positive
I often begin my Turning Adversity Into Opportunity speeches, workshops, classes, and trainings by asking participants to share something positive they're doing that is helping them.

Sharing what we're doing well—and the resources we have discovered that are helping us—can make it easier to talk openly and honestly about what we're not doing well and what's weighing most heavily on our hearts.

Staying connected through a new season
The relationship between aging parents and adult children is not a problem to be solved or a role reversal to be worked to perfection. It is a work in progress, to be tended with honesty, patience, respect, courage, and compassion.

When adult children ask rather than assume, offer support without taking over, make room for the differences they have with their parents, and generously offer their understanding and forgiveness, whenever possible, their aging parents are more likely to feel seen, heard, and loved. And when aging parents speak openly about what they need, what they fear, and what they hope for as they get older, their adult children and grandkids have a considerably better chance of navigating this challenging season of life together.

Communications such as the ones suggested in this post take courage. They can result in some of the most meaningful and important conversations a family will ever have. Taking time to understand one another better, doing our best to repair the kinds of sensitive matters that need repairing, and making peace with our parents will help all of us make the most of the precious time we have together.

Author’s Note: This post is adapted from my book, Raising an Aging Parent: Conversations for the Second Half of Life. It is the second installment in a three-part series exploring the changing dynamics of aging families. Part 1 explored Caring for an Aging Parent. Part 3 will examine sibling relationships and the role they can play in easing—or complicating—the challenges families face as their parents age.
